title: My Daughter Offered Me Her Basement for $800 a Month Plus Four Days of Babysitting a Week, So I Quietly Rented My Own Little House for $550
fb_text:
She wanted $800 a month and four days of babysitting every week for a basement room. I thanked her politely, then went and found a little house of my own for $550.

It happened on a Saturday afternoon, right after lunch.

We were sitting around Michelle's kitchen table when her husband, Todd, pushed a sheet of notebook paper toward me. A single figure was written in the middle.

$800.

He had drawn two circles around it.

"That covers your room, the bills, and part of the food," Michelle explained. "Plus, you'd watch the children four days each week. That way, you're contributing something, Mom."

Contributing something.

I'm sixty-seven years old. I raised Michelle on the modest income her father earned as a hired farmhand. This coming March will mark two years since my husband, Dale, passed away. If he had been sitting at that table, I know exactly what he would have thought of that paper. But he wasn't there anymore.

Todd stared at the salt shaker instead of looking at me.

My Social Security payment is $1,640. I spent twenty-two years handling accounts at the local lumberyard, so I could do the math without writing anything down. They wanted nearly half my monthly income. In exchange, I'd get a basement room with one tiny window, barely bigger than a cake pan, and a dehumidifier humming in the corner.

"Could I take another look at the room?" I asked.

We went down thirteen stairs. The air smelled like wet cardboard mixed with detergent. My four-year-old granddaughter, Sadie, came down with us.

"Grandma, are you going to sleep in the underneath?" she asked.

"Maybe, sweetheart. We'll see."

I wanted to refuse right there. But telling your only daughter no while sitting in her kitchen can quickly turn into a fight. And Michelle is the only child I have.

So I smiled. "Thank you, honey. I'll give it some thought."

I folded Todd's paper and put it in my handbag.

I didn't have much time to decide. I needed to move out of the farmhouse before November first. The house had come with Dale's job, and after his death the Olson family had kindly let me stay another two years. But their son was returning to work the farm, bringing his wife and a new baby. They needed the house. I understood completely.

On my way home, I stopped at the feed store four blocks away. For three weeks, Mr. Brandt had kept a handwritten notice taped beside his cash register.

Small house available. Two rooms and bathroom. Ask Brandt.

I asked whether it was still vacant, and he took me to see it. The little place stood on a quiet street behind the grain elevator. It had white siding, a porch swing, and only one step up to the front door. Harvest was underway, so a fine layer of corn dust covered nearly everything.

Mr. Brandt scratched his head. "It's nothing fancy, Judy."

I looked at the front entrance. "It's got its own door. That's enough for me."

"Rent's $550. Electricity is separate."

I wrote out the deposit check against the hood of my Buick. He handed me two keys on a metal ring, one for the front door and one for the back. For the first time in my life, I was holding keys to a home I had picked entirely for myself.

I waited nine days before telling Michelle. I know I should have spoken up sooner, but I was afraid of hurting her feelings. Then Todd happened to drive past the little house on his way to the plant and recognized my car.

Michelle called that evening.

"So you'd rather hand your money to a complete stranger than help your own family?"

I took a moment before answering. "I'd rather be your mother than somebody paying rent to you."

She ended the call.

For the next ten days, I heard nothing. No messages. No calls. Not even a photograph of the grandchildren. Every evening I sat on my porch swing and watched the grain trucks waiting to be weighed. I had my own home, my own keys, my own front door. But I missed my grandchildren so badly that some nights I wondered whether independence was worth the loneliness.

Then, on Thursday evening, just before supper, I heard a pickup stop outside. A door slammed. Michelle climbed out of the passenger seat, her eyes swollen and red as though she'd been crying for hours.

Todd followed her toward the porch, holding a yellow legal pad. The first page was filled from top to bottom with his handwriting.

I opened the screen door before they could knock.

Todd looked straight at me. "Judy, I'm the one who came up with that $800 figure. Michelle didn't."

He walked inside, set the legal pad on my kitchen table, and turned it to face me.

"There's something here you need to read."

article_html:
My daughter offered me a basement room for $800 a month from my Social Security check, plus four days of babysitting every week to "earn my keep." I thanked her politely, then found myself a little two-room rental near the grain elevator for $550.

The Paper on the Kitchen Table

It happened on a Saturday afternoon, right after lunch. We were sitting at Michelle's kitchen table when her husband, Todd, pushed a sheet of notebook paper toward me. One figure sat in the middle, circled twice: $800.

"That covers your room, the bills, and part of the food," Michelle said. "Plus, you'd watch the children four days a week. That way, you're contributing something, Mom."

Contributing something. I'm sixty-seven. I raised Michelle on what her father earned as a hired farmhand, and this March will be two years since Dale passed. Todd stared at the salt shaker instead of at me.

My Social Security is $1,640. After twenty-two years handling accounts at the lumberyard, I didn't need a pencil. They wanted nearly half my income for a basement room with a window the size of a cake pan and a dehumidifier humming in the corner.

We went down thirteen stairs. The air smelled of wet cardboard and detergent. Four-year-old Sadie followed us. "Grandma, are you going to sleep in the underneath?"

"Maybe, sweetheart. We'll see."

I wanted to say no right then, but Michelle is my only child, and a refusal in her kitchen could turn into a fight. So I smiled, said I'd think about it, and tucked the paper into my handbag.

Keys of My Own

I had until November first to leave the farmhouse. It had come with Dale's job, and the Olsons had kindly let me stay two extra years, but their son was coming home with his wife and a new baby. I understood.

On the way home I stopped at the feed store, where Mr. Brandt had kept a notice beside his register for three weeks: Small house available. Two rooms and bathroom. Ask Brandt.

The house stood on a quiet street behind the grain elevator, with white siding, a porch swing, and one step to the front door. Corn dust covered everything.

"It's nothing fancy, Judy," Mr. Brandt said.

"It's got its own door. That's enough for me."

The rent was $550, electricity extra. I wrote the deposit check on the hood of my Buick and took two keys on a metal ring. For the first time in my life, I held keys to a home I had chosen entirely for myself.

Silence

I waited nine days to tell Michelle, afraid of hurting her. Then Todd drove past on his way to the plant and recognized my car.

Michelle called that evening. "So you'd rather hand your money to a complete stranger than help your own family?"

"I'd rather be your mother than somebody paying rent to you."

She hung up. For ten days I heard nothing, not even a photo of the children. Each evening I sat on the porch swing watching grain trucks wait to be weighed, and some nights I wondered if independence was worth the loneliness.

The Yellow Legal Pad

Then, one Thursday just before supper, a pickup stopped outside. Michelle climbed out, her eyes red and swollen. Todd followed her up the walk carrying a yellow legal pad, its first page covered in his handwriting.

"Judy, I'm the one who came up with that $800 figure," he said. "Michelle didn't."

He set the pad on my kitchen table and turned it toward me. It was page after page of numbers: the mortgage, the truck payment, childcare, medical bills. His hours at the plant had been cut months earlier, and he had hidden how far behind they were. At the bottom of the first page he had written, Ask Judy for $800, and underlined it.

"I was scared," he said, looking at me at last. "I looked at your check and saw a way out, and I never asked what it would cost you. I'm ashamed of that."

Michelle wiped her face. "I should have asked questions. I just went along because I didn't want to see how bad it was. Then you said you'd rather be my mother, and I knew you were right."

I turned to the last page. Todd had written a different plan. They would talk to a counselor about their debts. He would take extra shifts. And nothing in it asked me for money.

"You don't owe us a cent, Mom," Michelle said. "If you ever want to watch the kids, it's because you want to."

I took her hands. "I never wanted to turn you away. I wanted to be asked, not charged."

I made the three of us supper that night in my own kitchen. The next Tuesday, I chose to watch Sadie and her brother for an afternoon, and nobody wrote a number on anything. Sadie asked if my house had an "underneath."

"No, sweetheart," I told her. "Just a front door, and it's always open to you."
